title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Deployment and Day‑2 Operations Playbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference best practices for private deployments (VPC-hosted and on-prem), reference architectures, packaging guidelines, Day‑2 operations, and upgrade/rollback procedures. It is intended for platform engineers, solutions engineers, and customer SREs responsible for onboarding and operating Private deployments.

Audience

- Platform/infra engineers who run Redwood Private instances
- Customer SREs responsible for production operations
- Solutions engineers performing initial deployments and handoffs

Goals

1. Provide repeatable deployment patterns for VPC and on‑prem environments.
2. Standardize Day‑2 operational tasks (monitoring, backups, capacity).
3. Define safe upgrade and rollback procedures with preflight checks and post‑upgrade validation.
4. Offer a compact customer requirements library for pre-sales and implementation scoping.

Prerequisites and Assumptions

- The customer has provisioned an admin VPC, network peering or transit gateway (if discussed), and appropriate IAM roles.
- Host systems meet minimum resource profiles in the Reference Architectures section.
- A private control plane (managed or self-hosted) is available; this playbook assumes connectivity between control plane and runtime agents is allowed by network policies.

Reference architectures (summary)

Table: Typical reference architectures and when to use them

| Architecture | Applies to | Key components | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small VPC (single-AZ) | PoC, dev | 3-node worker, 1 control VM, single NAT/ELB | Use for trials; no HA guarantees |
| Multi-AZ VPC (production) | Most customers | 6+ workers across AZs, HA control plane, managed DB (Aurora/RDS), LB per region | Recommended for production workloads with SLA |
| On‑prem cluster (Kubernetes) | Regulated/air-gapped | K8s 1.27+, node pools (gpu/cpu), offline package registry, private KMS | Requires packaging + air-gapped checklist |

Minimum compute profile (production)

- Control plane: 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB SSD (journaled), single reserved EIP for public control plane access (if applicable)
- Runtime worker (CPU-only): 8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 200 GB SSD
- Runtime worker (GPU): depending on GPU class (A100/80GB recommended for large models); baseline node: 16 vCPU, 256 GB RAM, 2 TB NVMe

Network and security baseline

- Control plane ports: 443 (HTTPS), 8443 (gRPC TLS), 9000 (metrics, optional behind LB)
- Worker agents: outbound HTTPS to control plane, gRPC/TLS endpoints for task assignment
- KMS/HSM: TLS endpoints reachable from control plane and runtime nodes
- TLS: mutual TLS between control plane and agents enforced by default
- RBAC: use least privilege; separate service accounts for control plane, backup jobs, and operators

VPC deployment guide (step-by-step)

1) Preflight checklist
   - Confirm VPC CIDR and available IPs for node pools.
   - Ensure NAT/gateway, route tables, and security groups are configured for outbound connectivity.
   - Provision database (managed or self-hosted) and confirm encryption-at-rest.
   - Provision KMS key and test encrypt/decrypt via API.

2) Control plane installation (managed/self-hosted)
   - For managed control plane, provide the control-plane endpoint and install the agent on customer nodes.
   - For self-hosted: deploy control plane as HA deployment (3 replicas), connect to managed DB, configure LB with health checks (HTTP 200 on /healthz).

3) Worker bootstrap
   - Use the official installer or Helm chart to join workers to the control plane. Example Helm values (simplified):

```yaml
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: redwood/runtime-worker
  tag: v2026.02.0
nodeSelector:
  workload: runtime
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "4000m"
    memory: "32Gi"
  limits:
    cpu: "16000m"
    memory: "128Gi"
```

4) Model storage and caching
   - Configure object storage (S3-compatible); provide read/write credentials to control plane.
   - Enable prefix caching for frequently used models; set TTLs based on workload (default 24h).

5) Validation and smoke tests
   - Run the following checks: control plane /healthz, worker registration list, a 1-request latency test for a 512-token generation, embedding request test.
   - CLI smoke example: redwoodctl health-check --endpoint https://control-plane.example.com

On‑prem packaging and air‑gapped deployment considerations

- Packaging: provide a release tarball containing OCI images (tarred), Helm charts, and a signed manifest. The manifest is verified with the release public key.
- Registry: mirror required images to the local registry and update Helm values.repository to point to internal registry.
- KMS/HSM: if using on-prem HSM, coordinate key import and test with the control plane.
- Time sync: enforce NTP/PTP for cluster nodes.
- Offline install steps (summary):
  1. Import images to local registry.
  2. Apply CRDs and Helm charts from local files.
  3. Run smoke tests using local endpoints.

Day‑2 operations (daily/weekly/monthly runbook)

Daily checks
- Dashboard health: check per-route latency P50/P95, error rate, and queue length.
- Agent count: ensure expected number of registered workers; alert if < 90% of target.
- Core service health endpoints: control plane, scheduler, cache service.

Weekly tasks
- Disk usage sweep on model cache nodes (> 70% triggers eviction policy review).
- Verify backups completed for config DB and model metadata.
- Validate canary traffic and model quality metrics for any deployed rollouts.

Monthly tasks
- Capacity planning review using token consumption reports, 95th percentile latency, and utilization.
- Run a simulated failover (control plane single replica removal in staging).

Operational playbook: incident triage (short)

1. Identify scope: determine whether issue is control plane, runtime, model, or network.
2. Collect artifacts: logs from control-plane pods, worker logs, metrics (Prometheus), recent deploys.
3. Mitigate: scale up workers, enable fallback model variant, or toggle routing policy to a lower-cost region.
4. Postmortem: add to incident tracker and link to postmortem page in confluence.

SLOs and alert thresholds (recommended defaults)

- Regional request success rate: 99.9% monthly
- P95 inference latency: < 350ms for small models, < 1200ms for long-context models (default target)
- Control plane API error rate: < 0.1% per minute

Upgrade and rollback procedures

Pre-upgrade checklist
- Verify backups for DB and model metadata exist and are valid.
- Confirm canary environment is running and smoke tests pass on the new release (use tag vYY.MM.patch).
- Notify stakeholders and schedule a maintenance window if required.

Rolling upgrade steps (recommended for HA clusters)
1. Start with control plane canary: deploy a single replica of the new control plane version in canary namespace. Run integration smoke tests for 1h.
2. Gradually roll control plane replicas (1 by 1) with readiness probe pass required before moving to the next replica.
3. Upgrade worker nodes using a rolling restart strategy and cordon/drain pattern.
4. After workers are upgraded, run end-to-end validation including: latency test, throughput test (small batch), and a model correctness spot-check.

Rollback criteria and steps
- Criteria: elevated error rate (>0.5%), P95 latency regression > 2x baseline, or failed smoke tests after > 30 min.
- Steps: if criteria met, stop the rollout and roll control plane/workers back to previous image tag. Use the previously validated DB snapshot if schema changes are incompatible.

Example rollback commands (Kubernetes)
- kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane --to-revision=<previous>
- kubectl set image deployment/runtime-worker runtime-worker=redwood/runtime-worker:v2025.11.3

Customer requirements library (scoping checklist)

Use the checklist below during the pre-sales or kickoff call. Mark items as MUST/HAVE/NICE:

1. Network and connectivity
   - Public control plane acceptable? (MUST/HAVE)
   - VPN/Direct Connect or Transit Gateway required? (MUST/HAVE)
   - CIDR ranges and NAT requirements (MUST)

2. Data residency and encryption
   - Required regions for data residency (MUST)
   - KMS/HSM integration and key rotation policies (MUST)

3. Compliance and logging
   - Audit log retention (MUST)
   - SOC2/ISO artifacts required (HAVE)

4. Capacity and performance
   - Expected QPS and per-request token distribution (MUST)
   - Latency SLOs and traffic patterns (MUST)

5. Operational responsibilities
   - Who owns system upgrades and patching (Redwood / Customer)? (MUST)
   - Pager and escalation contacts (MUST)

Ownership, contacts and escalation

- Default owners: Platform Engineering (owner), Solutions Eng (customer onboarding), Customer SRE (day-to-day ops).
- Escalation path: on-call -> platform lead -> engineering manager -> VP Eng. Include customer-facing on-call rotations in the deployment runbook.

Appendices

A. Example diagnostics commands
- redwoodctl list-workers --endpoint https://control-plane.example.com
- kubectl logs -n redwood control-plane-0
- curl -sS https://control-plane.example.com/healthz | jq

B. Example alerting rules (Prometheus-style summary)
- alert: ControlPlaneHighErrorRate
  expr: rate(control_plane_http_errors_total[5m]) > 0.005
  for: 2m
  labels: { severity: "page" }
